posts.author: HazMatch3
posts.body:
Hi all! First time poster here.
I've become infatuated with the "Anomaly Game" genre over this past year. I recently just played Route 8 and Platform 8 (sequel to Exit 8), and decided I wanted to take the plunge and make my own in RPG Maker. The way I have it mapped out in my head is I would just make different "rooms" with 2 buttons. Essentially one button for "Anomaly present" and one button for "room is normal" (if that makes sense). I would then attach events so if you pressed the wrong button it would take you back to the starting point and if you guessed right then it would take you to the next randomly selected room.
My problem is this method is unreliable in the sense that I don't know how to make the levels select randomly. As well as missing a counter to let the player know how close they are to the "end". Not to mention if I had only one "starting room" with preset events, then would I have to make multiple versions of the "starting room" just so that they could mix with the anomaly rooms and keep the player guessing. Etc, Etc.
So my questions are as follows: Is this an efficient development path to go down? Is there a more efficient path to take to streamline development and improve the quality of the overall experience? Are there plugins that would help in the making of this type of game? What engine would be best for this? (I have MV, MZ, and XP). And really any other advice you guys may be able to provide.
Previous experience in Anomaly games would help because i'm sure my explanations would make more sense if you already have an idea what these games typically play like. Thank you guys in advance, and I hope I posted this in the right place!

I can see I messed up here. So I will explain now.
An Anomaly game functions like this:
The player will enter an environment. (Ex. In Route 8 you are driving on a road). In this environment you are presented with some characteristics that resemble what the environment "normally" looks like. When you get from one end to the other, the game will send you back to the beginning of the environment and you do that all over again. The difference is as you progress in this continuous loop, the characteristics of the environment will have differences that the play starts to notice. These differences in characteristics are called "Anomalys". These anomalys can range anywhere from the sky being a different color, to a monster chasing you, to a billboard having a different design, etc etc. These games will also typically have a mechanic in order for the player to actually progress to the "end". This mechanic typically works as follows (I will use Route 8 again as an example):
If an anomaly is present, turn right.
If no anomaly is present, turn left.
If the player guesses correctly, they will (essentially) move on to the next "level". Rinse and repeat this process until they reach a pre-determined "end". (In many games, this is the 8th level). If the player guesses incorrectly, they will be sent back to "level 0" and have to guess correctly however many times to get to the "end". (Again, this would typically be 8 times. The developer can do however many they want though. 8 is just a common number many of these games that I have played use.)
It is important to note that these anomalys are preset by the Dev, but when they appear is completely randomized. You can do a run and have no anomalys present for 4/8 levels (uncommon but it can happen), then do a second run and have an anomaly in 7/8 levels.
That is the gist of what these type of games entail. I apologize for not providing this information in advance, and I hope this explanation helps clear things up a bit. If I need to explain anything further I have no problem doing that.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
That mechanc can be done purely by eventing, and with only two variables: one for the progress and one for the randomizer (reused each screen).
In the randomizer, you will have o9ne number for each possible anomaly (1-?) and then decide how the chances for a "normal" screen are above that - you don't have to set it to 50% (same amount) and you can even enter random "normal" changes here.
The scene would then have many events conditioned to the variable to make the spites appear at different predetermined places to create the scenes. Might take some learning for all the eventing tricks, but basically simple again.
then one or two events to check input, and if the rolled random for the screen is lower or higher than the cutoff between anomaly and normal. if it fits, increase progress variable if not set it to 0
One hint:
